summary: Describes how link-state routing protocols interact with traffic engineering tunnels to create IGP shortcuts. It explains how Dijkstra's shortest path first algorithm can be adapted so routes are calculated over those tunnels.

plainLanguage.summary: Traffic engineering tools build explicit routes through a network, which are called tunnels. Routing protocols normally ignore them and send traffic hop by hop. RFC 3906 shows how a link-state router can be taught to use a tunnel as the first step of a route, so that the traffic follows the path the traffic engineers built.

questions: how do routing protocols use tunnels
what is an igp shortcut over a te tunnel
how does the spf calculation change with te tunnels
subtitle: How a link-state router can send its traffic down a traffic engineering tunnel instead of hop by hop.

tldr.problem: Traffic engineering calculates explicit routes through a network, but the ordinary link-state routing protocols still send traffic hop by hop along the cheapest path they can see, ignoring those tunnels.
tldr.mechanism: The memo changes one step of the shortest path calculation. When the router reaches a node that is the far end of a tunnel it owns, it uses the tunnel as the first hop instead of the neighbouring router, and downstream nodes inherit that first hop.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo describing one algorithm. It adds a way to set a manual cost on a tunnel so that traffic can be pushed onto it, left on the native path, or split between them.

today: RFC 3906 is an Informational memo published in October 2004, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes one way for a link-state IGP to use traffic engineering tunnels, and it leaves the creation of the tunnels themselves to RFC 2702 and RFC 3209.

sections.title: Tunnels and Shortest Path Routing
sections.content:
Link-state protocols such as IS-IS and OSPF use Dijkstra's SPF algorithm to compute a shortest path tree to all nodes in the network. Routing tables are derived from that tree, and they hold tuples of destination and first-hop information. When a router does normal hop-by-hop routing, the first hop is a physical interface attached to the router.

Traffic engineering algorithms work differently. They calculate explicit routes to one or more nodes in the network. At the router that originates those explicit routes, they can be viewed as logical interfaces that supply Label Switched Paths through the network. This memo calls those paths Traffic Engineering tunnels, or TE-tunnels, and cites RFC 2702 and RFC 3209 for the capabilities that create them.

Whether the tunnels exist and how traffic is switched over them are separate questions. A node may define static routes pointing to the TE-tunnels, it may match the recursive route next-hop with the TE-tunnel end-point address, or it may define local policy such as affinity based tunnel selection. The mechanism described here is different: it uses link-state IGPs to install IGP routes over the tunnels dynamically.

The tunnels under consideration are those created explicitly by the node doing the calculation, with an end-point address known to that node. It does not matter for the algorithm whether the tunnel is strictly or loosely routed. One constraint keeps the mechanism loop free: when a router chooses to inject a packet addressed to a destination D, it may inject the packet into a tunnel whose end-point is closer, according to the link-state IGP topology, to D than the injecting router is. In other words, the tail-end of the tunnel has to be a downstream IGP node for the destination.

The mechanism assumes the tunnels have already been set up, and they may be there for quality of service, bandwidth, redundancy, or fast reroute reasons. The memo warns that applying an IGP shortcut over them means the physical traffic switching may not match the original traffic engineering goal, and that traffic patterns change over time, so some measurement of the forwarding plane and feedback into the tunnel attributes are needed to keep the network efficiently engineered.
sections.plainLanguage: A link-state router normally works out the cheapest path to a destination and sends each packet to the next router along it. A traffic engineering tunnel is a path that was worked out in advance and set up through the network. This memo describes a way to make the router start that path at the tunnel instead of at the neighbouring router.

sections.title: How the Shortest Path Calculation Changes
sections.content:
During each step of the SPF computation a router discovers the path to one node. If that node is directly connected to the calculating router, the first-hop information is derived from the adjacency database. If the node is not directly connected, it inherits the first-hop information from its parent or parents. Each node has one or more parents, and each node is the parent of zero or more downstream nodes.

For traffic engineering purposes, each router maintains a list of all the TE-tunnels that originate at that router. For each of those tunnels, the router at the tail-end is known.

When the router finds the path to a new node, that is, when the node is moved from the TENTative list to the PATHS list, it must determine the first-hop information. There are three ways to do this. First, examine the list of tail-end routers directly reachable via a TE-tunnel: if there is a TE-tunnel to this node, use the TE-tunnel as the first hop. Second, if there is no TE-tunnel and the node is directly connected, use the first-hop information from the adjacency database. Third, if the node is not directly connected and is not directly reachable via a TE-tunnel, copy the first-hop information from the parent node or nodes to the new node.

The result is that traffic to nodes that are the tail-end of TE-tunnels flows over those TE-tunnels, and traffic to nodes downstream of the tail-end nodes does too. If there are multiple TE-tunnels to different intermediate nodes on the path to a destination, traffic flows over the TE-tunnel whose tail-end node is closest to that destination.

Some applications need both the native adjacency and the TE-tunnel next-hop information for the tail-end and its downstream nodes. The head-end node may then conditionally switch the data traffic onto TE-tunnels based on user defined criteria or events, split the flow of traffic towards either type of next hop, or install the routes with two different types of next hops into two separate RIBs. Multicast protocols running over physical links may have to perform RPF checks using the native adjacency next hops rather than the TE-tunnel next hops.
sections.plainLanguage: Only one step of the calculation changes. When the router has worked out a path to a new node, it looks at three things in turn: is the far end of one of my tunnels this node, then use the tunnel; is the node directly attached to me, then use the normal link; otherwise, use whatever the parent node uses. Because the last case copies the parent's answer, everything downstream of a tunnel automatically uses the tunnel too.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The SPF algorithm finds equal-cost parallel paths to destinations, and the enhancement described in the memo does not change that. Traffic can be forwarded over one or more native IP paths, over one or more TE-tunnels, or over a combination of the two.

The memo walks through a small topology: rtrA, rtrB and rtrC in a line, with rtrD joined to rtrB and rtrE joined to rtrD and rtrC. All links have the same cost, and a TE-tunnel is set up from rtrA to rtrD. When the SPF calculation puts rtrC on the TENTative list, rtrA realizes that rtrC is not directly connected, so it uses the first-hop information from the parent, which is rtrB. When the calculation on rtrA moves rtrD from the TENTative list to the PATHS list, it realizes that rtrD is the tail-end of a TE-tunnel, so rtrA installs a route to rtrD via the TE-tunnel and not via rtrB.

When rtrA puts rtrE on the TENTative list, it realizes that rtrE is neither directly connected nor the tail-end of a TE-tunnel, so it copies the first-hop information from the parents, rtrC and rtrD. Traffic to rtrE now load-balances over the native IP path rtrA, rtrB, rtrC and over the TE-tunnel from rtrA to rtrD.

Where both parallel native IP paths and paths over TE-tunnels are available, implementations can let the network administrator force traffic to flow over only TE-tunnels, or only over native IP paths, or let both be used for load sharing.
sections.plainLanguage: The example has five routers and a tunnel from the first to the fourth. The router at the first end sends traffic for the fourth router down the tunnel, and traffic for the fifth router is split between the tunnel and the ordinary path, because the fifth router sits behind both.

sections.title: Tuning the Cost of a Tunnel
sections.content:
When an IGP route is installed with a TE-tunnel as the next hop, the question arises of what the cost or metric of that route should be. The most obvious answer is to assign a metric the same as the IGP metric of the native IP path, as if the TE-tunnels did not exist. The memo's example: rtrA can reach rtrC over a path with a cost of 20, and X is an IP prefix advertised by rtrC, so the route to X is installed in rtrA's routing table with a cost of 20. When a TE-tunnel from rtrA to rtrC comes up, by default the route is still installed with a metric of 20; only the next-hop information for X changes.

While that scheme works well, in some networks it is useful to change the cost of the path over a TE-tunnel, to make the route over the tunnel less or more preferred than other routes. Where equal cost paths exist over a TE-tunnel and over a native IP path, adjusting the cost of the path over the tunnel can force traffic to prefer the tunnel, to prefer the native IP path, or to load-balance among them. Where multiple TE-tunnels go to the same or to different destinations, adjusting TE-tunnel metrics can force traffic to prefer some tunnels over others, regardless of the underlying IGP cost to those destinations.

Setting a manual metric on a TE-tunnel does not impact the SPF algorithm itself. It only affects the comparison of the new route with the existing routes in the routing table, which can be IP routes to another router advertising the same IP prefix, or a path to the same router but through a different outgoing interface or a different TE-tunnel. All the routes to IP prefixes advertised by the tail-end router are affected by the TE-tunnel metric, and so are the metrics of paths to routers that are downstream of the tail-end router.

The mechanism is loop free, because the TE-tunnels are source-routed and the tunnel egress is a downstream node for the computed destinations. The end result of TE-tunnel metric adjustment is more control over traffic loadsharing. If there is only one way to reach a particular IP prefix through a single TE-tunnel, then no matter what metric is assigned, the traffic has only one path to go. The routing table described in this section can be viewed as the private RIB for the IGP, and the metric is an important attribute of the routes in it, because a path with a lower metric is selected over the other paths for the same route.

The metric of a TE-tunnel can be represented in two ways. An absolute, or fixed, metric means the cost of the IP routes in the routing table does not depend on the topology of the network. The fixed metric is used not only for the cost of the IP routes advertised by the router that is the tail-end of the TE-tunnel, but also for all the routes downstream of that tail-end router: if there are TE-tunnels to two core routers in a remote POP and one of them is assigned an absolute metric of 1, then all the traffic going to that POP will traverse this low-metric TE-tunnel. A relative metric is merely an adjustment of the dynamic IGP metric as calculated by the SPF computation, so the cost of the IP routes in the routing table is based on that metric. A relative metric can be a positive or a negative number. Not configuring a metric on a TE-tunnel is a special case of the relative metric scheme, since no metric is the same as a relative metric of 0. The memo adds that the relative metric is bounded by the minimum and maximum allowed metric values, and that a positive metric disables the TE-tunnel in the SPF calculation.

The example topology for these adjustments has IP prefixes X, Y and Z advertised by rtrC, rtrD and rtrE, a TE-tunnel T1 from rtrA to rtrC, and an IGP metric of 10 on every link. Without the tunnel, rtrA installs routes X, Y and Z with metrics 20, 30 and 40. With T1 up and a relative metric of -5 on it, the three routes are installed with metrics 15, 25 and 35. With an absolute metric of 5 on T1, they are installed with metrics 5, 15 and 25.
sections.plainLanguage: A route that uses a tunnel still has a cost, and that cost decides whether the router prefers it or the ordinary path. By default the cost is the same as the ordinary path would have been, so the tunnel only changes the next hop. Setting a cost by hand lets an operator push traffic onto the tunnel, keep it off, or split it between them, without changing the shortest path calculation itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states that it does not change the security aspects of IS-IS or OSPF, and that the security considerations specific to each protocol still apply. It points to RFC 3567 on IS-IS cryptographic authentication and to RFC 2328 for OSPF.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo changes nothing about how the routing protocols authenticate themselves, so the security rules that already apply to IS-IS and OSPF still apply.

viz.caption: THE THREE FIRST-HOP DECISIONS MADE DURING SPF

items.title: Tunnel first
items.text: Examine the list of tail-end routers reachable through a TE-tunnel. If there is a TE-tunnel to this node, use the TE-tunnel as the first hop.

items.title: Adjacency second
items.text: If there is no TE-tunnel and the node is directly connected, take the first-hop information from the adjacency database.

items.title: Parent third
items.text: If the node is neither directly connected nor directly reachable through a TE-tunnel, copy the first-hop information from the parent node.
